receipts.first_text_witness: You know that moment when you check your savings account and see $847 sitting there and instead of feeling proud, you just feel defeated, like you're throwing pennies into the Grand Canyon, hoping it'll eventually fill up. You've been saving for months, maybe even a year, cutting back on coffee, skipping dinners out, living like a financial monk, and for what? a number that couldn't even cover a decent emergency, let alone make you feel wealthy. Meanwhile, your friend with zero savings just bought a new PlayStation and seems genuinely happier than you do. And you start thinking, "What's the point? Why am I torturing myself for this pathetic pile of cash that feels about as powerful as a wet napkin in a hurricane?"
receipts.last_text_witness: Not just your bank account, but how you see yourself and what you believe you're capable of. That $10,000 becomes the down payment on a completely different financial life. If this video helped you understand why those early dollars feel so pointless, and more importantly, why you should keep going anyway, hit that like button, and let me know in the comments where you are in your journey to 10,000.

primary_source_receipts.locator: CFPB "Financial well-being in America" (2017) as summarised by Consumer Finance Monitor, Aspen Institute and Brookings
primary_source_receipts.finding: Liquid savings showed the largest difference in financial well-being scores of any factor examined (under $250: average 41; $75,000+: 68); described by a former CFPB research lead as the variable most highly correlated with well-being; liquid savings do not protect against larger or persistent shocks.
primary_source_receipts.limitations: Report not read directly; correlational; no threshold analysis retrieved.
